newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian refugees pay first visit to Serb enclave.
newsitem.headline: Croatian refugees pay first visit to Serb enclave.

text.p: Croatian refugees from Eastern Slavonia paid a visit to the Serb-held enclave on Friday for the first time in years to pay respect to their dead for All Saints Day.
Eastern Slavonia was seized by minority Serbs in mid-1991 when they rebelled against Croatia's independence from Yugoslavia and expelled thousands of non-Serbs from the region.
The area was put under U.N. Transitional Administration (UNTAES) control in January, after the Croatian army recaptured other Serb-held enclaves. It should revert to Croatian rule sometime in 1997.
"This is the beginning of our return... Next time we'll go back for good," said 62-year-old refugee Vladimir Cacic who was boarding a bus near the Croatian town of Osijek.
The U.N. tried to strip the event of political significance but refugees said they wanted to use the occasion to see the homes they fled five years ago.
"I haven't been to my village for so long," said Zuzana Romer, 52, whose mother is buried at one of the cemeteries. "I am going there to see my home too."
Some 40 buses carrying more than 2,000 refugees crossed over to Serb-held territory on Friday morning escorted by UNTAES, the U.N. civil police, and joint Croat-Serb police patrols.
Men and women, some dressed in black and carrying flowers, were allowed a one-hour visit to 30 grave sites scattered all over Eastern Slavonia, where UNTAES said it could guarantee their safety.
Every year thousands of Croatian Roman Catholics visit graves of their loved ones on All Saints Day.
Fearing incidents, UNTAES banned journalists from visiting the graves, saying it was a "purely religious event".
Eastern Slavonia saw some of the worst battles of the 1991 Croatian-Serb war and inter-ethnic hatred is still running high.
"I am not afraid," Cacic said. "Actually I feel great to be able to go back after five years."
"Still I told him to eat his breakfast this morning because it could be his last," his friend Romer added with a laugh.
"Seriously, we don't expect any incidents, but we know well who we are dealing with," Cacic added.
UNTAES spokesman Phil Arnold told Reuters the visit had gone smoothly up to midday and no problems were reported.
